HEARD:  February 5 & 6; April 1
& 2; May 13 & 26; August 4, 11, 12 & 27; September 13 & 20; December
2 & 7, 2004; January 25 & 28, February 17 & 22, April 29,
September 27, & December 23, 2005.

lampkin J.:

[
1
]

Bruce Mandell is charged with the following
offences on two informations being tried together on consent:

(i) that
between the months of July and October, 2002 at the Town of Markham, knowing
that Jannet Madhosingh is harassed or being reckless as to whether Jannet
Madhosingh is harassed, he did without lawful authority repeatedly follow
Jannet Madhosingh from place to place; repeatedly communicate directly or
indirectly with Jannet Madhosingh; beset or watch the residence of Jannet
Madhosingh; engage in threatening conduct directed at Jannet Madhosingh thereby
causing Jannet Madhosingh to reasonably, in all the circumstances, fear for her
safety, contrary to
section 264(1)
and
(2)
of the
Criminal Code
;

(ii)
that on or about the 12
th
day of November 2002 at the Town of
Markham he did, being at large on his recognizance entered into before a
justice and being bound to comply with a condition of that recognizance
directed by the said justice, fail without lawful excuse to comply with that
condition to wit: abstain from communicating directly or indirectly with Jannet
Madhosingh or any immediate family members, contrary to
section 145(3)
of the
Criminal
Code
;

(iii)
two counts that on or about the 13
th
day of November 2002, at the Town
of Markham he did, being at large on his recognizance entered into before a
justice and being bound to comply with a condition of that recognizance
directed by the said justice, fail without lawful excuse to comply with that
condition to wit: abstain from communicating directly or indirectly with Jannet
Madhosingh or any immediate family members, contrary to
section 145(3)
of the
Criminal
Code
.

FACTUAL BACKGROUND

[
2
]

At the time of her testimony in April 2004,
the complainant Jannet Madhosingh was 50 years old. At that time she had been a
high school teacher for 26 years. She is very well educated. In 1976 she
completed a Bachelor of Arts (Honours) degree at Carleton University. In 1989
she obtained her Master of Arts degree in Hispanic studies, linguistics and psychology
at the same University. I infer from her evidence and a list of her telephone
numbers filed as an exhibit concerning which she mentioned her ‘ex’, that she
was married to Barry Hubah who lives in Trinidad and that she is divorced.

[
3
]

She has one daughter, Brandi-Lee Hubah, who
was born on the 28
th
day of January, 1979. Ms. Hubah is a registered
nurse. She graduated from university in June 2002. Mother and daughter reside
together in Ms. Madhosingh’s townhouse at 33 Harris Way in Thornhill. The townhouse
is part of a condominium complex known as Johnsview Village.

[
4
]

Bruce Mandell was born on August 14
th
,
1949. In 1981 he was married to Janet Mandell. They have one son, Myles. The
family lives at 28 Valloncliffe Road, Thornhill, a few blocks away from Ms.
Madhosingh, according to Mr. Mandell a two or three minute drive away.

[
5
]

Mrs. Mandell has been in the real estate
business since 1979. Mr. Mandell joined her in the business in 1981 and they
work as partners for the same real estate brokerage company, Coldwell Banker
Pinnacle Real Estate. Their names appear together on the same business card as
‘Bruce M. Mandell’ and ‘Janet Schulberg’. Mr. Mandell testified that he has
been a very successful real estate agent.

[
6
]

Ms. Madhosingh was introduced to Bruce Mandell
in or about April 1999 by her neighbour whose house Mr. Mandell had sold.
Thereafter he visited Ms. Madhosingh and at the end of May 2001 they entered
into a personal relationship.

[
7
]

Mr. Mandell said that the date of the start
of the relationship was May 28
th
, 2001. He testified that he met Ms.
Madhosingh and her daughter by chance at Longo’s Grocery situate at Bayview
Avenue and Laureleaf Road near to their respective homes on Saturday May 26
th
,
2001. When they were out in the parking lot, Ms. Madhosingh left her daughter
and approached him and asked him if he wanted to have a carnal relationship.

[
8
]

On the other hand Mrs. Patricia Daley, of
whom more will be heard in these reasons, testified under cross-examination
that Mr. Mandell told her that he had pursued Ms. Madhosingh for a year and she
totally ignored him. I accept Mrs. Daley’s evidence and reject Mr. Mandell’s
version that Ms. Madhosingh, almost out of the blue approached him in the
parking lot on May 26
th
, 2001 and told him that she wanted to have a
carnal relationship with him. Moreover he testified under cross-examination
that he first had sexual intercourse with Ms. Madhosingh in August 2001. It
seems most unlikely that someone who had made such a proposition would wait for
two to three months before entering into full sexual relations.

[
9
]

He testified further that on Monday May 28
th
,
2001 he went to Ms. Madhosingh’s home and they went for a coffee. He testified
further that the very first night they had sexual contact. He told her that he
and his wife, although living together under the same roof, were not sleeping
together, that they were distant physically and emotionally and that separation
between him and his wife was imminent.

[
10
]

During the relationship they saw each other
almost every day. They called each other on their cell phones and had long
conversations at all hours of the day and night. A few months prior to July
2002 Mr. Mandell told Ms. Madhosingh that he would give her an engagement ring
to show how committed and sincere and trusting he was. Sometime between July 17
th

and 28
th
, 2002 he went to her house to give her a ring. At first she
refused to accept it because she was no longer interested in having a committed
relationship. He left the ring on the table in the house. Eventually she did
put the ring on. She told him that it meant for her her freedom from him and as
long as they had that understanding, it would be okay to do whatever she wanted
with the ring.

[
11
]

On June 28
th
, 2002 Ms. Madhosingh
listed her home at 33 Harris Way, Thornhill, for sale with Coldwell Banker
Pinnacle Real Estate with Mr. Mandell as the agent. The commission on sale was
originally set at 4% of the sale price but was reduced the same day by an
amending agreement to 3%.

[
12
]

Mr. Mandell was asked in his examination in
chief the following question to which he gave the following answer:

Q.

Why are you aware of why Ms. Madhosingh had decided
to list her property for sale?

A.
I led her to believe ah – that ah – we would live together and um –
that was the only reason the property was for sale and I can say also that the
property has never been listed since.

[
13
]

She gave dates of July 2
nd
or 3
rd

and July 8
th
, 2002 as the termination of the physical relationship
between them, Ms. Madhosingh testified that from July 2002 there was no sexual
contact between her and Mr. Mandell, except on one occasion when he kissed her
and she pushed him away. I accept her evidence in this respect. On October 6
th
,
2002 Mr. Mandell wrote out and signed a seven-page document in which he
professed,
inter alia,
his love for Ms. Madhosingh. Paragraph 8 of the
document is to the following effect:

Although
we have
not been
intimate for sometime (I don’t recall exact date) its (
sic
)
been several months, it is agreed and understood that upon signing these statements
our
love
and
committment
(
sic
) for each other
shall
never be questioned again.
This shall be
absolute proof
once and for
all. We have had problems but everybody does, but there will never be a
question of the deep love we have for each other. (Emphasis in the original).

[
14
]

But she still continued to see him. In the
meantime she had called the police on him and the police had warned him to keep
away from her. On August 4
th
, 2002 about 4:45 a.m. Constables Robin
Shaw and Paul Wilson attended the residence of Ms. Madhosingh who lodged a
complaint that she had ended a relationship with Mr. Mandell and that he had
just been at her residence and had continually been going back to her residence
and bothering her although she had asked him to stop. She asked that police go
and caution him about his behaviour. Ms. Madhosingh indicated to the police
that she did not feel that her safety was in jeopardy and only wanted her ‘ex’
cautioned about his behaviour. He was more of a nuisance.

[
15
]

The officers then attended at the Mandell
residence at 5:06 a.m. Mr. Mandell answered the door and stepped outside.
Constable Shaw warned Mr. Mandell against his continually contacting Ms.
Madhosingh even though she had asked him not to and told him that his behaviour
could be considered criminal harassment.

[
16
]

Mr. Mandell was surprised that police should
go to his home. He said that he understood and that he did not believe that he
had done anything wrong. He stated that he would not contact Ms. Madhosingh
anymore. He requested that police not attend at his home in the future.

[
17
]

The officers spent about five minutes at Mr.
Mandell’s home. Constable Wilson testified that they then parked at the end of
Mr. Mandell’s street. Mr. Mandell approached them and spoke with Constable
Shaw. Constable Wilson did not recall the conversation but believed that Mr.
Mandell was seeking some clarification. Constable Shaw testified that after she
returned to the station, she received a telephone call from Mr. Mandell about
5:45 a.m. He wanted clarification as to what would constitute criminal
harassment and she explained that to him.

[
18
]

When he returned to their room, Mrs. Mandell
asked her husband why police had attended. He lied to her and told her that a
vendor of a listing that he had, had complained that he was being a nuisance.
She asked to see the file and saw that it concerned a townhouse at 33 Harris
Way about a mile from their home. She made him promise to drop the listing.

[
19
]

Sometime in August 2002 Mr. Mandell left the
following handwritten note between the doors of Ms. Madhosingh’s residence:

Please
put your message box on ASAP. I know you have a very busy life, but from time
to time you must be updated or in the alternative a phone call would be nice,
or an answering machine. I thank you in advance. This way you don’t need to
speak to anyone who (
sic
)

you have no time for. Since you are
busy now obviously, could you be available all day Sunday early start, or
whatever is good for you if anything. Please advise. Thank you.

[
20
]

Ms. Madhosingh had shut off her voice mail
messaging service because Mr. Mandell continued to misuse it and he could not
get in touch with her to relay to her appointments for her real estate and she
had no answering machine on her residential line. She told him if he did not
contact her to cancel the appointments.

[
21
]

On Sunday October 6
th
, 2002 Ms.
Madhosingh called Mr. Mandell. She understood that there was an incident in her
condominium corporation complex involving him the night before. He suggested
that they meet. He wanted to provide her with written documentation about something
very personal. They met at the Pickle Barrel around mid-day.

[
22
]

He told her that he had parked facing her
house for three hours and had fallen asleep in his car. The security attendant
gave him a parking ticket for parking in the fire route. He asked that she
speak to the security company and explain that he had a legitimate reason to be
there. He told her that he was waiting to see who was taking her home. She was
not at home that night.

[
23
]

Mr. Mandell left a photocopy of the Parking
Infraction Notice of the Town of Markham in her mailbox - she does not recall
when – and asked that she look after it. It was issued by Carlos Dalosta on
October 5
th
, 2002 at 12:49 a.m. against the vehicle bearing Plate
No. ALLJ 042 for parking in a fire route. The infraction carried a fine of
$100.00.

[
24
]

In October 2002 Matthew Warner was a
security guard and private investigator employed by Shadow International Inc.
His duties were to patrol the grounds of Johnsview Village, the condominium
complex housing Ms. Madhosingh’s townhouse. As a result of information received
from Constable Wilson and a member of the Board of Directors of Johnsview
Village, Mr. Warner was on the lookout for a white Cadillac sedan, Licence
Plate No. ALLJ 042.

[
25
]

On October 5
th
, 2002 Mr. Warner
located the vehicle at 8:41 p.m. It was the same vehicle that had been ticketed
at 12:49 that morning by Carlos Dalosta. The vehicle was parked on the shoulder
near to 33 Harris Way, Ms. Madhosingh’s townhouse. Mr. Mandell was seated in
the driver’s seat but got out of the vehicle. Mr. Warner noted that he was wearing
a black, full-length woollen coat and black shoes. Mr. Mandell did not appear
to be wearing any pants but Mr. Warner conceded in cross-examination that he
could not see what was underneath the coat. Mr. Warner issued a notice pursuant
to the
Trespass

to

Property

Act
of Ontario to Mr.
Mandell not to return to the property. Mr. Mandell refused to sign the notice
acknowledging receipt of it and he refused to take the notice.

[
26
]

Mr. Mandell remained in his car. Mr. Warner
called his dispatcher and requested that Constable Wilson attend. Constable
Wilson did attend. Mr. Mandell’s car was pulled into 33 Harris Way driveway.
Constable Wilson could not say what, other than a long coat, Mr. Mandell was
wearing.

[
27
]

Constable Wilson asked Mr. Mandell if he
remembered being at his residence on August 4
th
, 2002 when he was
cautioned. Mr. Mandell told him that there had been difficulties before but
that the relationship had rekindled. Constable Wilson knocked on Ms. Madhosingh’s
door and called her telephone but no one answered. Mr. Mandell left the
premises at 9:07 p.m.

[
28
]

On October 6
th
, 2002 Mr. Mandell
also presented to Ms. Madhosingh two type written letters, one to her
condominium corporation and the other to Shadow Security. The contents of the
letter were to the effect that she would like the charges against him dropped because
he was a friend of hers. Her name was typed at the bottom for signature. She
refused to sign the letters, which she considered to be insulting.

[
29
]

At their meeting of October 6
th
,
2002 Mr. Mandell presented a seven-page hand written document on legal size
paper. It purports to be a statement commencing ‘I Bruce Michael Allan
Mandell’. It had all been written out when he gave it to her. The document
refers to their sexual relationship which he hoped she would resume, his offer
to help her purchase a car, reducing Coldwell Banker’s commission on the sale
of her home to 0% on certain terms, and his confirmation of his love for her.
She did not agree with the terms of the document, which she viewed as an
attempt to pressure her into resuming their sexual relationship. He gave her a
photocopy of the document, which she did not sign. He told her to think about
it and give him a response later.

[
30
]

Ms. Madhosingh’s daughter wanted to use her
car. Mr. Mandell told Ms. Madhosingh that if she went with him for coffee, he
would give her a termination of the real estate listing agreement. She took her
car home for her daughter who dropped her off at Tim Horton’s at the corner of
Woodbine Avenue and John Street. Mr. Mandell picked her up there and they went
for coffee on Yonge Street. Instead of the termination of the listing agreement
he gave her a document typewritten on a single sheet of letter size paper which
had several amendments made in handwriting by Mr. Mandell. It reduced the
commission of the Listing Broker (Coldwell Banker Pinnacle Real Estate) to 0%
of the selling price, and a commission of 2½ % for the co-operating or selling
broker. They both signed the agreement and witnessed each other’s signature.

[
31
]

After coffee she asked Mr. Mandell to drop
her off on Bayview Avenue, which he did between 8:00 and 9:00 p.m. She walked
to her residence and Mr. Mandell went south on Bayview Avenue. Within five to
ten minutes of her arrival home, Mr. Mandell called her asking that she go and
help him because they wanted to arrest him. He said that he was in front of her
house. She went out and found him with the security guard.

[
32
]

That night at 9:41 p.m. Mr. Warner spotted
Mr. Mandell on the premises again. He was standing outside of his car near 43
Harris Way, down the street from 33 Harris Way. Mr. Warner placed Mr. Mandell
under arrest for trespassing. Mr. Warner read his right to counsel to Mr.
Mandell who told him that he understood his rights and did not wish to call a
lawyer. The police were called and two police officers attended at 9:49 p.m.,
one of whom was Constable Wilson. Mr. Warner turned Mr. Mandell over to them.

[
33
]

Constable Wilson spoke with Ms. Madhosingh
who was standing outside 33 Harris Way. She said that things were fine between
her and Mr. Mandell and there were no concerns for her safety. Mr. Warner told
Constable Wilson that the trespass notice still stood due to other area
residents’ complaints regarding Mr. Mandell. Constable Wilson released Mr.
Mandell unconditionally and told him that he was not to return to the property
until the property manager told him that he could.

[
34
]

I reject Mr. Mandell’s evidence that Ms. Madhosingh
had told him to take some paper to their meeting on October 6
th
,
2002, and that she dictated most of the seven-page document that he signed. He
said that he wanted to go to the bathroom even before they had started and he
left for that purpose and when he returned he found that she had left the restaurant
with the document. It must have taken some time to write out the document in
long hand and give her the letters that he wanted her to sign to get him off
the hook with respect to the parking violation and the trespass notice. He
would have gone to the bathroom before he started on that lengthy procedure.

[
35
]

Throughout this period Ms. Madhosingh was
still in telephone contact with Mr. Mandell. She said that he forced her on one
occasion to go with her to Whitby when she was due early at school. He blocked
her car in the garage. She said he virtually kidnapped her. All she had to do
was to re-enter her home and call the police. Another time they went to Harbour
Front, she said to look at properties. Another was a trip to Grand Bend. He
gave her and her daughter a lift down to Toronto to see The Lion King. She said
the relationship was professional at that time. They met at Costco Grocery
where they shopped because she did not have a Costco Card and he had one. I
accept that the sexual relationship was over. It is a reasonable inference to
draw that Mr. Mandell was doing his best to woo her back into a sexual
relationship as the seven-page document dated October 6
th
, 2002
clearly shows.

[
36
]

Ms. Madhosingh was determined to end the
relationship because there was nothing between them except for the listing
agreement to sell her house. She asked him to draw up an agreement to terminate
the listing. She had also heard from relatives and friends that he had been calling
them and visiting them in an attempt to locate her which he confirmed to her.
In the week leading up to October 19
th
, 2002 he went to her school
and she swore at him. She was angry. She met with him at a café on Markham Road
to try to convince him not to return to her school for safety reasons.

[
37
]

She tried to get his brother and mother to
meet with her so that she would not have to deal with the matter. It was too
much for her to bear and she felt in many ways responsible for a lot of his
actions. The meeting never materialised. He had led Ms. Madhosingh to believe
that his brother and mother knew about their relationship. He had introduced
Ms. Madhosingh briefly to his mother at the Pickle Barrel.

[
38
]

She met with him at a restaurant called
Montana’s in the Steeles Avenue East and Highway 404 area. She did not feel
that she had convinced him how frightened he had made several people, including
herself, her daughter and her school environment. He confided in her that he
had been married before to his present wife’s sister and because she was out of
control, that marriage lasted about 17 months. He told her that he too had a
problem with control, which was a source of difficulty in his current marriage.
They were at the restaurant for about half an hour. She may have spoken to him
again that night.

[
39
]

There was telephone contact between them
during the week. She had called him and begged him not to go to her school. And
he did not. On Saturday October 19
th
, 2002 they spoke on the
telephone and agreed to meet at his office at 5:00 p.m. with respect to the termination
of the listing of her house.

[
40
]

At the meeting he pleaded with her to go to
a hotel or for dinner or coffee. She declined. She finally got the Termination
of the Multiple Listing Agreement. He told her that the relationship will never
end, that he would always love her. She told him that she just wanted to be
free and independent as she was before she had met him.

[
41
]

Before she left he told her that he had
something for her in his car. He got a card from his car. The card was a
sentimental card asking whether they could make a fresh start and hold on to
their memories. He signed and dated it. He drew a heart beneath his signature
and inserted their initials in the heart with an arrow pointing to the word
‘Forever’. She thanked him and left. The meeting lasted about half an hour.

[
42
]

As she was leaving he ran out to his car and
started to follow her. He pulled up beside her and asked to go and meet his
brother for coffee. Initially she did not wish to go but she pulled into a lot
near to his office where there was a coffee shop. He approached her and told
her that it was too far for his brother to come. She told him she wanted to go
home and that she would meet his brother some other time. He had parked
horizontally behind her and would not move. He was blocking traffic in the lot
and others were blowing their horns to get him to move. He directed them which
way to go.

[
43
]

She eventually agreed to meet his brother.
He said she should follow him and she did so for a short time. They went onto
Steeles Avenue westbound. He turned to go south on Bathurst Street. She
followed. He called her on her cellular phone and pulled alongside her and said
that he wanted to see her face.

[
44
]

About two stop lights south of Steeles
Avenue she began to feel unsafe. Her instinct told her that she was putting her
life on the line. She needed to go home. She was in the right lane and turned
right at the light. She went into the parking lot of a construction site. He
was on her left and he also turned right and blocked her car. He was in the
middle of the street and again blocking traffic.

[
45
]

She was able to turn her car around to face
the street he was parked on. He got out of his car and was approaching her but
other motorists were calling on him to move. He went in front of his car and
was directing traffic. She was able to ease behind him and get back onto
Bathurst Street to go north as she had the green light. He jumped back in his
car, reversed and spun around in the intersection and followed her.

[
46
]

She was intending to turn on to Steeles
Avenue to go eastbound to go home. He got on the inside lane and she could not
turn. She continued north on Bathurst and he continued to drive alongside of
her and to block her on the right side.

[
47
]

She got ahead of him and was able to turn
right onto Clark Avenue. He turned behind her. She continued in the right lane.
He was able to get ahead of her. As they approached Charles Avenue the light
was red. Ms. Madhosingh eased her car onto the left lane so that she would be
behind him rather than beside him.

[
48
]

Mr. Mandell got out of his car and went to
the driver’s side window of Ms. Madhosingh’s car and asked her to go for
coffee. Her window had been half way down but she turned it up when he went to
her window. He asked her to go for coffee. She said she needed to go home. He
said: ‘You’re not going on a date’.

[
49
]

Ms. Madhosingh said at that point Mr.
Mandell jumped on the hood of her car. His hands were on her windscreen and his
whole body was lying on the hood of her car with his hands on the windscreen.

[
50
]

She steered the car to the right lane hoping
that he would get off. She went just beyond the light and he still did not get
off. When she noticed that he was still there she stopped. He held onto the
windshield wipers when she stopped. Less than a minute later she was
rear-ended. He flew off the hood.

[
51
]

Ms. Elizabeth Brandon teaches literacy to
adults. She was eastbound on Clarke Avenue about 5:30 or 5:45 p.m. on October
19
th
, 2002 approaching the intersection of Clarke Avenue and Charles
Avenue. She was in the right hand lane. Clarke Avenue has two eastbound and two
westbound lanes. The light in her lane was not working. She glanced over to
make sure it was a green light. When she glanced back she realised that the car
ahead of her was not moving. She did not see any brake lights. She slammed on
her brakes but still hit the car. The accident occurred just past the
intersection.

[
52
]

When her vehicle hit the car she saw a man
fall off onto the ground but her vision was blinded at that point. She jumped
out of her car and noticed a man on the ground in front of the car she had hit.
He was towards the left. He jumped up – she was surprised that he got up so
quickly. She asked both him and the driver of the car if they were all right.
The man walked past her. She thought he was in shock. She asked both parties several
times. When she did not get a reply she went to her car and sat.  She
identified the man as Mr. Mandell. Her car was a write-off.

[
53
]

Later the driver of the car she had hit went
over to her and asked if she was all right. The man walked around and
eventually he also asked how she was. He said he was not going to make a big
deal about it.

[
54
]

Kenneth Ramelson is self-employed in the
computer industry. On October 19
th
, 2002 in the late afternoon he
was driving westbound on Clarke Avenue. He saw a car with a man whom he
identified as Mr. Mandell leaning over the hood and windshield of a car on the
driver’s side. Mr. Mandell was sprawled over the windshield, his left arm was
towards the passenger side holding on to the windshield wiper and his right
hand was on the post between the driver’s door and the windshield.

[
55
]

The car was a little east of the traffic
light on Clarke Avenue. Mr. Mandell’s feet were on the ground and he was
leaning forward. The car was stationary, not moving. Mr. Ramelson told his wife
that if the car did not move someone would hit it, and that’s what happened.

[
56
]

Mr. Ramelson made a U turn and stopped. He
asked the lady in the car that was hit if she was okay and she said that she
was fine. She did not express fear for her safety.

[
57
]

At the rear of the car he asked Mr. Mandell
if he was okay and he said he was. Mr. Ramelson told Mr. Mandell that he was
calling the police. Mr. Mandell asked him not to but he did anyway. Mr. Mandell
told him that the lady in the car that was hit was his lady and that everything
was fine.

[
58
]

Mr. Ramelson saw a cream coloured Cadillac
parked at the traffic light in the left lane before the intersection - that is
west of the intersection and before going through it. No one was in the
Cadillac. After he called police Mr. Mandell moved the Cadillac into the right
lane east of the intersection and parked behind Mr. Ramelson.

[
59
]

Mr. Mandell said that at the end of the
meeting on October 19
th
, 2002 Ms. Madhosingh agreed to meet his
brother. They were to go to California Sandwiches in the Allen Road and
Sheppard Avenue area. He could not reach his brother. Ms. Madhosingh became upset
and said that she was going to tell his wife everything. He pleaded with her not
to do that.

[
60
]

They drove along Clarke Avenue in Thornhill.
At the corner of Clarke Avenue and Charles Street he got out of his car to
speak to her at the red light. He was behind her but in the passing lane. There
were a couple of cars between them.  When he went to the driver’s side window,
she turned her head towards the passenger side. He was asking that she not go
to his wife and upset her.

Every criminal trial involving an offence
against the person who has suffered some loss or damage also gives rise to
civil proceedings for damages. Whether the offence was for wrongful death,
assault, fraud or criminal harassment. The fact that most complainants probably
do not issue proceedings does not mean they do not have the right to do so.
There is an age-old maxim at common law: “
ubi jus, ibi remedium
” – where
there is a right, there is a remedy.

[
83
]

The right exists whether the defendant in
the criminal proceedings is found guilty or the charge against him is
dismissed. A defendant in criminal proceedings who is acquitted may well be
mulcted in damages in civil proceedings for the same wrong for any number of
reasons, not the least of which is the different standard of proof: in criminal
proceedings, the standard is proof beyond a reasonable doubt which is somewhat
approaching certainty:
R. v. W. (D.)
(1991)
1991 CanLII 93 (SCC)
, 63 C.C.C. (3d) 397;
R.
v. Lifchus
(1997)
1997 CanLII 319 (SCC)
, 118 C.C.C. (3d) 1;
R. v. Starr
(2000)

2000 SCC 40 (CanLII)
, 147 C.C.C. (3d) 449. On the other hand in civil proceedings, the standard is on
a balance of probabilities, a lower standard of proof.

[
84
]

What is more, unless the defendant pleads
guilty to the charges and therefore admits liability, the complainant
(plaintiff in the civil proceedings) has to prove the case in the civil proceedings.
The complainant/plaintiff can’t simply file a Certificate of a finding of guilt
and hope to succeed. The Rule in
Hollington v. Hewthorn
[1943]
K.B. 587;
[1943] 2 All.E.R. 35
, has been the subject of much criticism. In that
case it was held that a conviction for careless driving was inadmissible as
evidence in subsequent civil proceedings against the driver and his employers
because the conviction merely represented the opinion of the criminal court.
The judgment recognised that a conviction for murder would likewise be
inadmissible as evidence of the commission of the crime in subsequent civil
proceedings. This drove the well known Canadian scholar, C.A. Wright, to comment
(21 Canadian Bar Review):

To
state that a civilised community is willing to see a man hanged on such a
finding of fact but to treat such a finding as a mere opinion in a subsequent
case involving a matter of dollars and cents is a reflection on the
administration of justice as well as an offence to common sense.

[
85

Nevertheless the Rule in
Hollington v.
Hewthorn
remains a rule of evidence in Anglo-Canadian law. That is not
to say that civil proceedings commenced during the prosecution of criminal
proceedings can never be taken into consideration during the course of the
criminal proceedings. I well recall a trial for assault before me in which a
husband was the defendant and his wife the complainant. Family Law proceedings
were ongoing at the same time. The complainant had sworn to an affidavit in the
Family Law proceedings, which was directly contradictory to the evidence before
me. I allowed the affidavit to be filed as an exhibit in the criminal proceedings
and allowed the wife to be cross-examined on it.

The crime of criminal harassment is dealt
with in
section 264
of the
Criminal Code
, the first two subsections of which
enact as follows:

Section
264. (1) No person shall, without lawful authority and knowing that another
person is harassed or recklessly as to whether the other person is harassed,
engage in conduct referred to in subsection (2) that causes that other person
reasonably, in all the circumstances, to fear for their safety or the safety of
anyone known to them.

(2) The conduct
mentioned in subsection (1) consists of

(a)
repeatedly following from place to place the other person or anyone known to
them;

(b)
repeatedly communicating with, either directly or indirectly, the other person
or anyone known to them;

(c)
besetting or watching the dwelling house, or place where the other person, or
anyone known to them, resides, works, carries on business or happens to be; or

(d)
engaging in threatening conduct directed at the other person or any member of
their family.

[
88
]

Within recent years the higher courts have
given trial courts guidance with respect to this crime.

[
89
]

In
R. v. Sillipp
(1997),
1997 ABCA 346 (CanLII)
, 120
C.C.C (3d) 384, 11 C.R. (5
th
) 71, the Alberta Court of Appeal held
that the
mens

rea
required for the offence is that the accused
knew that his conduct caused the complainant to be harassed or that he was
aware of such risk and was reckless or wilfully blind as to whether or not the
person was harassed. Honest mistake is a defence to the offence. Foresight of
the prohibited consequence of causing actual fear is not required in order to
hold the accused responsible for the results of the unlawful activity.

[
90
]

It must be proved however that:

(i) the accused has
engaged in conduct set out in s. 264(2)(a), (b), (c) or (d);

(ii) the
complainant was harassed;

(iii)
the accused who engaged in such conduct knew that the complainant was harassed
or was reckless or wilfully blind as to whether the complainant was harassed;

(iv)
the conduct caused the complainant to fear for his or her safety or the safety
of anyone known to the person; and

(v) the
complainant’s fear in all the circumstances was reasonable.

[
91
]

A single incident can constitute threatening
conduct. Harassment is proven if as a consequence of the prohibited act, the
complainant was in a state of being harassed or felt harassed in the sense of
being tormented, troubled, worried continually or chronically, plagued,
bedevilled and badgered:
R. v. Kosikar
(1999), 138 (3d) 217,
1999 CanLII 3775 (ON CA)
, 178
D.L.R. (4
th
) 238 (Ont. C. A.);
R. v. Ohenhen
(2005)

2005 CanLII 34564 (ON CA)
, 200 C.C.C. (3d) 309.

[
92
]

The words “tormented, troubled, worried
continually or chronically, plagued, bedevilled and badgered” are not
cumulative and are individually synonymous with the word “harassed”.
Establishing any of these factors can constitute harassment:
R. v.
Kordrostami
(2000),
2000 CanLII 5670 (ON CA)
, 143 C.C.C. (3d) 488, 47 O.R. (3d) 788 (C.A.).

[
93
]

Harassment should not be given a restricted
definition and includes”requests, solicitations, incitements” that have the
effect of bothering someone because of their continuity or repetition:
R.
v. Lamontagne
(1998),
1998 CanLII 13048 (QC CA)
, 129 C.C.C. (3d) 181 (Que.C.A.).

dates, times and locations that she would be seeing Mr. Mandell in the future?

A.
Yes, I did.

Q.
And you recommended that she do that?

A.
Yes.

Q.
And I’m sure that as in the course of your duties in investigating
this that day, you also told her if there’s anything that happens in the future
in terms of sightings, she should report that to the police.

A.
I probably did, yes.

Q.
Okay. That would be something that you would do in the ordinary
course of your duties, dealing with this type of call?

A.
Correct.

(vi)
She delivered a letter dated February 12
th
, 2003 to the police directed
to Detective Godber and asked that it not be disclosed to the Crown. The letter
was really a series of questions seeking clarification of a number of issues
and indicating that she would like to withdraw her daughter from the case
because she feared for her daughter’s safety and wanted to spare her the
turmoil. She probably was under the impression that Mr. Mandell had been
charged with criminal harassment of her daughter also which was not the case.
Indeed after Ms. Madhosingh had testified the Crown applied to amend the
information to have the daughter as a complainant but her daughter had already
testified. After argument I denied the Crown’s application. I find nothing
objectionable about the letter except the paragraph immediately following her signature,
which is to the following effect:

We
live in the big city. There is a shooting every day. We can’t wait till the
shooting is over to attend to Bruce Mandell. He is more dangerous than that
criminal. There is more chance of Bruce killing me or my daughter than a thug
with a gun. This is a life changing experience for us. I cannot do it without
you. Let’s make the time. Confidence in one another is critical.

If anything the paragraph shows the
deep fear that Ms. Madhosingh has of Mr. Mandell.

[
144
]

I find as a fact that the Crown has proved
the case of criminal harassment beyond a reasonable doubt. Although Ms.
Madhosingh had discontinued all sexual contact with Mr. Mandell as of July 8
th
,
2002 she nevertheless continued an association with him. They did go out. He
took her to various functions. He did not physically force her to go with him
but he certainly used much more than mere moral suasion. She avoided him as
much as she could. He frantically looked for her calling and visiting her
family and friends in search of her. On one occasion he even called her at her
sister’s home in Windsor. The writing was on the wall for all to see. Just as
he testified that his wife told him after his arrest that he was not listening
to her with respect to keeping away from Ms. Madhosingh, in the same way he was
not listening to what Ms. Madhosingh was telling him that ‘It’s over’.
Alternatively he was wilfully blind. I find that the Crown has proved beyond a
reasonable doubt the elements of the offence as set out in
s. 264(2)
(a), (b)
and (c) of the
Criminal Code
.

[
145
]

I am further satisfied that Ms. Madhosingh
was tormented, troubled and constantly worried by Mr. Mandell’s behaviour and
he knew or ought to have known that his behaviour was having that effect upon
her. The mere fact that she was avoiding him ought to have driven home that
fact to him.

[
146
]

As time wore on, her fear increased. That
fear crystallized on October 19
th
, 2002. His behaviour that day
proved that Mr. Mandell was prepared to do anything, including putting her
safety and his own safety in jeopardy to win her back. Her fear was reasonable.

[
147
]

There is no doubt that Mr. Mandell is a
master of deceit. He was able to deceive his wife to whom he had been married
for 25 years and presumably knew him better than anyone else. His wife
testified that there has not been a day in their relationship that they did not
tell each other that they loved each other several times a day. They had been
together for more than half of her life and there had never even been a hint that
he would be having a relationship behind her back.

[
148
]

He was able to deceive Ms. Madhosingh for 14
months. He told her how much he loved her too, that there was no one else for
him, that he was going to leave his wife and be with her. He gave her a ring as
a token of his affection for her and a sign that they were engaged and would be
married. But all the time he was using her as a sex object.

[
149
]

After the accident on October 19
th
,
2002 Mr. Mandell went home, his wife did not recall what time. He did not go up
to her but stayed downstairs. He phoned up to her and said: “Honey, I’ve just
got some paper work to do. Do you mind if I watch the game?” She told him that
was okay. There was no mention of a car accident. When he went up she was already
asleep.

[
150
]

The next morning Mr. Mandell got up before
his wife and went to the Emergency Department of North York General Hospital.
His wife did not see him before he left. After examination Dr. Robert Riddle
diagnosed that he was suffering from a mild concussion. He told the doctor that
he had fallen down and said nothing about being involved in an accident with
Ms. Madhosingh because he was concerned that somehow his wife would find out
that he was having an affair.

[
151
]

After his visit to the hospital he went home
to change. His wife said something unusual happened. While she was doing his
hair, he put his arms around her waist and pulled her and said: “I want you to
know that I love you more than anything in the world.” She asked: “What are you
hiding? Fess up.” He only told her: “I love you.”

[
152
]

With respect to the breaches of recognizance
I find that Mr. Mandell had a clear operating mind when he called Ms.
Madhosingh on November 12
th
and 13
th
, 2002. He was in a
predicament looking for help from her. Following his arrest on the criminal
harassment charge on October 20
th
, 2002, he got his mother to lie to
his wife as to his whereabouts. When his wife found out that he was in jail and
not with his mother’s boyfriend she made arrangements with a lawyer and stood
as surety for him to be released. It was not until November 14
th
,
2002 that his wife knew of his involvement with Ms. Madhosingh – although she
had told him on August 4
th
, 2002 when the police visited their home,
to get rid of the listing. He lied to Dr. Riddle, the doctor in the Emergency
Department at North York General Hospital, saying that he had suffered a fall
and he lied similarly to his family doctor, Dr. Shapiro.

[
153
]

His defence with respect to the breaches of
recognizance is that he was impaired and did not know what he was doing. He
consulted four doctors - Dr. Riddle, Dr. Shapiro and Dr. Cooper, who are
medically qualified, and Dr. James Long, a Doctor of Philosophy, who was
qualified as an expert in clinical psychology and neuropsychology and permitted
to give opinion evidence in those areas. They all agreed that Mr. Mandell had
suffered a mild concussion as a result of the fall/accident. Mr. Mandell was
never hospitalised. He suffered headaches following the accident and was prescribed
Advil and Tylenol, well known over-the-counter painkillers.

[
154
]

Dr. Cooper is a psychiatrist. Part of his
report issued on Mr. Mandell is as follows:

Mental
examination revealed a tall well-groomed man in a suit. He was pleasant and
co-operative and very articulate. He was anxious and tense. At times during the
session he appeared to be sad-looking but was able to compose himself. There
was no evidence of thought or perceptual disorder. He was oriented in all
spheres. Memory was intact. His concentration was intact. He was of bright, average
intelligence. Judgment was intact.

[
155
]

Dr. Long testified as follows in
re-examination:

Judgment
is a function of thinking that results in a decision concerning some issues and
it relies on memory, it relies on the ability to collate the data that’s related
to it and then come to an appropriate condition as decision. But of course
there’s good judgment and bad judgment and here we’re simply talking about
judgment and whether it’s – when a person is reporting in a test like I gave
Mr. Mandell, it related to whether his judgment was effective or not and his
ability to make judgments and the indication was that it was not as good as it
has been.

[
156
]

The problem is that Mr. Mandell’s
judgment after the accident was just as poor  as it was before the accident. And
no one is suggesting that he did not know what he was doing for all the months
he was having an affair with Ms. Madhosingh. It is well nigh impossible to find
a crime that does not involve poor judgment on the part of the perpetrator.

[
157
]

No doctor has said that he did not have an
operating mind. For sure he was anxious and worried. Who wouldn’t be in his
situation? But he had the perspicacity to lie to his doctors to keep the facts
from his wife. He had the perspicacity to lie to his wife. He had the perspicacity
to ask his mother to phone his wife and tell her he would not be home on the
night of October 20
th
, 2002 because he was with his mother’s
boyfriend when in fact he was in jail. He had the perspicacity to call Ms.
Madhosingh from Agincourt Collegiate, where she used to teach night school and
from a public telephone booth so that she would not know that he was the
caller.

[
158
]

I find as a fact that Mr. Mandell knew
exactly what he was doing when he made those phone calls to Ms. Madhosingh. He
was begging for help.

[
159
]

The Defence relies on a number of cases.
With respect to the crime of criminal harassment the cases relied upon simply
reiterate the elements of the offence as set out in the cases I have referred
to above. With respect to the breaches of recognizance the cases deal with the
issue of the
mens rea
and I find that he had the necessary intent to
make the phone calls to Ms. Madhosingh. I further find that he made all three
phone calls as Ms. Madhosingh testified.

[
160
]

There
will be findings of guilt with respect to all the offences on which Mr. Mandell
was arraigned.
